title: Introduction to Machine Learning
oneLiner: What machine learning is, when to use it, and the main ways a machine can learn from data.

what.html:
Machine learning (ML) is programming a computer by showing it examples instead of writing the rules yourself.

In traditional programming you give the computer data plus a program, and it gives you output. In ML you give it data plus the right outputs, and it gives you back the program (a model).

Everyday versionTeaching a child to recognise dogs. You don't write a rulebook ("four legs, fur, tail…"); you point at many dogs and say "dog". Eventually the child spots dogs they have never seen. That's ML.

A tidy definition from the slides: a program learns if its performance P on a task T improves with experience E.

why.html:
• Some rules are impossible to write down. Nobody can list the rules for recognising a face or a handwritten "7".
  • Some rules keep changing. Spammers invent new tricks weekly; a learned filter can be retrained, a hand-written rule list just grows.
  • Some answers must be personal. Your recommendations, your medicine dose.
  • But not always. Payroll has exact rules. If you can solve it with a formula, you don't need ML.

how.title: AI, data science and ML: who contains whom
how.html: AI is the big goal: machines that act intelligently. ML is one way to get there: learning from data. Data science overlaps both: collecting, cleaning and analysing data to make decisions, often using ML as a tool.

how.title: Learning = Task, Performance, Experience
how.html:
Every learning problem can be pinned down with three words:

Task TClassify emails as spam or not
Performance P% of emails classified correctly
Experience EEmails labelled by people

If you can't name all three, the problem isn't ready for ML yet.

how.title: Rules by hand vs rules learned
how.html:
Old spam filter: a person writes rules ("contains '4U' or 'free'") and keeps adding more. The list becomes long and fragile.

ML spam filter: show it labelled spam and normal mail; it finds the telling words itself, and can be retrained automatically as spam changes. The program is shorter, easier to maintain and usually more accurate.

how.title: Three ways to learn
how.html:
• Supervised: examples come with answers (feedback). Like studying with an answer key.
  • Unsupervised: no answers; find structure (groups) on your own. Like sorting a box of mixed buttons by look.
  • Reinforcement: no answers, only delayed rewards or penalties. Like a child learning that the stove is hot.

Sort the scenarios below into the right type.

how.title: Supervised: a category or a number?
how.html:
If the answer is a category (spam/not spam, benign/malignant) it's classification. If it's a number (price, temperature) it's regression.

The slides' simplest classifier: "if tumour size is above T, call it malignant". Learning means picking the best T.

how.title: Unsupervised: finding groups nobody labelled
how.html: Give the computer customer data with no labels and ask it to find groups (big spenders, occasional shoppers…). That's clustering. It can also compress many features into a few (dimensionality reduction) so you can visualise them.

how.title: Reinforcement: learning from rewards
how.html: An agent tries an action, gets a reward or a penalty ("Ouch! −50 points"), updates its strategy (policy), and tries again until it finds the best behaviour. Game-playing and robot control work this way.

how.title: In between: semi-supervised
how.html: Often you have a few labelled examples and a mountain of unlabelled ones. Semi-supervised learning uses both, e.g. a photo app that asks you to name one person, then finds them in all your photos.

how.title: Learn all at once or keep learning
how.html:
• Batch: train on all the data at once, then deploy.
  • Mini-batch: train on chunks.
  • Online: update the model one example at a time as data arrives, good for streams and changing trends.

how.title: Memorise examples or build a model
how.html: Instance-based learning keeps the examples and compares new cases to them ("this looks like those"). Model-based learning boils the data down to a formula and throws the examples away.

how.title: Tools and the accuracy vs explainability trade-off
how.html: scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras and Weka do the heavy lifting. As a rough rule, the most accurate models (deep learning, boosting) are the hardest to explain, while simple ones (linear regression, small trees) are easy to explain.

how.title: The ML workflow
how.html: Should I use ML? → gather data → clean and visualise → choose a model and loss → optimise → tune hyperparameters → analyse mistakes and iterate. The slides' demo predicts used-car price from mileage this way.

demo.html: The slides' demo case study in miniature. Four cars, mileage vs price. First try the laziest model: predict the same price for every car (a constant). Slide the guess and watch the total error. Then switch on the straight-line model and see how much better it does.

example.html:
Spam filtering. Task: label each email spam or legitimate. Performance: percentage classified correctly. Experience: a database of emails labelled by people. The model learns which words and patterns are typical of spam and is retrained as spammers change tactics.

Other examples from the slides: fraud detection, voice assistants, recommendations on shopping and streaming sites, self-driving cars.

misunderstandings: ML is the same as AI.
ML is one part of AI. Search, planning and logic are AI too.
Unsupervised learning has no test phase.
It often does: e.g. assign a new image to the nearest cluster centre.
More complex models are always better.
They may be more accurate but harder to explain and easier to overfit.
If exact rules exist (payroll), ordinary code is simpler and correct.
takeaways: ML learns a program from examples instead of hand-written rules.
A learning task is defined by Task, Performance measure and Experience.
Supervised (labelled), unsupervised (unlabelled) and reinforcement (rewards) are the three main types; semi-supervised mixes the first two.
Classification predicts categories; regression predicts numbers.
Use ML when rules are unknown, unexplainable, changing or personal, and follow the workflow from data to evaluation.
thirty: Machine learning means giving a computer examples and letting it work out the rules. A task is well defined when you can name the task, the performance measure and the experience it learns from. With answers in the data it's supervised learning: classification for categories, regression for numbers. Without answers it's unsupervised: finding groups or structure. With only rewards it's reinforcement learning. Use ML when rules are hard to write, keep changing or must be personalised.
